extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility under the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether patent claims recite eligible subject matter under the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG), including the Step 1 statutory category check, Step 2A determination of judicial exceptions, and Step 2B 'significantly more' analysis. Includes examples showing how to apply the tests to computer-implemented and GUI claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'Thus, the claim is directed to a process, which is one of the statutory categories of invention (Step 1: YES).' Perform Step 1 first to establish the claimed category before analyzing judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exception identification (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claim recitations (steps, concepts, limitations) to see if they are similar to concepts courts have identified as exceptions. Example: 'the claim recites comparing and organizing data for transmission. This is simply the organization and comparison of data which can be performed mentally and is an idea of itself.' Mark Step 2A YES if directed to an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize abstract-idea subtypes (mental processes, information-management concepts, mathematical algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize specific categories often treated as abstract: mental processes (organizing/comparing information), certain information-management concepts, and mathematical algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: 'comparing and formatting information is simply the organization and comparison of data which can be performed mentally'; mathematical algorithms (e.g., calculating a scaling factor from areas) are analogous to Benson, Flook, Grams. Use these analogies when identifying an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly more analysis (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether any element or combination of elements in the claim ensures the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider additional limitations individually and as an ordered combination to determine if they add significantly more. Example phrasing: 'The claim as a whole is analyzed to determine whether any element, or combination of elements, is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components are not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic computer hardware or generic computer functions (e.g., microprocessor, memory, transmitter performing receiving/processing/transmitting) do not by themselves amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language from examples: 'Generic computers performing generic computer functions, alone, do not amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.' Examiners should construe generic computer components at a high level of generality and explain why they are routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use or Internet limitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., 'over the Internet') does not by itself make the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Internet limitations are simply a field of use that is an attempt to limit the abstract idea to a particular technological environment and, so do not add significantly more.' Use this when an asserted improvement is merely tying the idea to the Internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered-combination can supply 'significantly more' if it provides a technological solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are conventional, their ordered combination can amount to 'significantly more' if the combination provides meaningful limitations or a solution rooted in computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From example: when taken as an ordered combination the limitations 'provide unconventional steps that confine the abstract idea to a particular useful application' and 'demonstrates a technologically rooted solution to an Internet-centric problem,' analogous to DDR Holdings. Use factual analysis of how the combination solves a technical problem (e.g., alerting offline subscribers by activating a viewer app via wireless channel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be analyzed for eligibility according to their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'All of the claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.' When construing claim scope, use BRI to determine whether recited elements are generic or limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble limitation rule (MPEP 2111.02): does the preamble limit?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim preamble merely states purpose/field of use (non-limiting) or gives 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim (limiting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance in examples: 'Where the preamble only states the purpose or the field of use of an invention, the preamble does not limit the scope of the claim... If the preamble gives “life, meaning and vitality” to the claim, it should be construed to limit the claim.' Apply MPEP 2111.02 when assessing whether preamble limitations can supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Office-action/allowance drafting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection or allowance, examiners should explicitly identify the exception and explain why claim limitations do or do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example examiner guidance: 'A rejection of claim 1 should identify the exception by pointing to the filtering, generating and formatting steps and explain that the comparing and formatting of information is a mental process... The rejection should also identify the additional limitations regarding the transmission server and explain why those limitations comprise only a generic computer performing generic computer functions.' For allowances, add remarks explaining why the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider elements individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether additional limitations amount to significantly more both when viewed individually and when viewed as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples repeatedly contrast viewing limitations 'individually' versus 'as an ordered combination' and instruct that either view can determine whether limitations add significantly more (e.g., individual limitations may be generic, but the ordered combination may produce an inventive, technological solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims necessarily rooted in computer technology that solve computer-specific problems may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention is necessarily rooted in computer technology and addresses a problem specifically arising in that technological environment (and supplies meaningful limitations), the claim may not be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the GUI relocating obscured textual information was found not to be directed to an abstract idea because it 'is necessarily rooted in computer technology to overcome a problem specifically arising in graphical user interfaces.' Use fact-based analysis showing the claim improves computer functionality or solves a technical problem.
